subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
I'm Francis, and I share a lab bench with Samir, so I see his group every day. There are five of them. They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler, and nobody else sits there. Nobody was told not to; it's just understood. They study in the back room of the library, split cab fares home at Diwali, and have a group name I've never heard said aloud.
They look comfortable. Nobody has to plan who to sit with. Nobody eats alone.
But last month the debate club put up a poster, and Samir stood in front of it for a long time. When I asked if he'd join, he laughed and said, "The guys would think I've gone posh." He didn't sign up. Maybe he didn't want to. I can't tell. But he looked back at the poster twice on the way out.

qa.q: Where does Samir's group eat lunch?
qa.a: They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling in front of the debate poster?
qa.a: Samir may have wanted to join but worried the group would judge him; looking back twice suggests he was torn, though Francis can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Samir do if the group starts to feel limiting?
qa.a: Samir could try the debate club anyway and mention it lightly to the group; a secure friendship can stretch to make room for other interests.

qa.q: How does the group look to Francis from outside?
qa.a: To Francis the group looks comfortable and closed at once: nobody eats alone, yet nobody else sits at that table.

grounding: Shows an outsider watching a settled friend group that shares everything, with both real comfort and quiet pressure not to look beyond it.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
Week one: Arnab, new to the college after a transfer, noticed the four girls straight away. Gopika and her friends walked into Economics together, sat in the same row every day, and passed one flask of tea along it.
Week three: They'd been to Darjeeling together over the long weekend; the photos were on every phone in class. Arnab asked Gopika if she wanted to join his statistics study circle. She glanced at the others before answering, "Maybe, let me see." She didn't come.
Week six: Gopika came to the study circle alone, late, and sat near the door. She was quick with the formulas and helped two people. After an hour her phone buzzed four times. She read the messages, said, "They're waiting at the canteen," and left, apologising twice. Arnab wondered whether she'd wanted to stay.

qa.q: What did the group pass along their row in Economics?
qa.a: They passed one flask of tea along it.

qa.q: What might Gopika's glance at her friends suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika felt she needed the group's okay, or worried how they would feel, before joining something outside it.

qa.q: What could help Gopika keep both her group and a new interest?
qa.a: Gopika could tell her friends plainly that she has the study circle for an hour and will meet them after, so the new commitment isn't treated as leaving.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Gopika's group over these weeks?
qa.a: Arnab sees warmth and closeness, but also a pull that brings Gopika back each time, and he wonders whether she wanted to stay.

grounding: Illustrates an outsider noticing over weeks how a close group's routines bring comfort and also an unspoken pull to stay inside it.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
Sonali, you ask why I didn't have close friends in my first year of college. Let me tell you what it looked like from where I sat.

There was a group of four in our hostel, Naren's lot. They ate at the same table every night, studied in the same room, took the same train home at Diwali. I used to watch them from two tables away and envy how easy it looked. They never had to ask, "Can I sit here?"

Once I asked Naren to join a trekking club with me. He wanted to. I saw it on his face. Then he looked at the others and said, "Nah, we have plans." Later I heard one of them tease him: "Trekking with Chetan now? Leaving us?"

It was comfortable, what they had. But I wondered if it was also a little like a room with the door shut.

qa.q: Who did Chetan ask to join a trekking club?
qa.a: Naren.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel watching Naren's group from two tables away?
qa.a: Chetan felt envious and a bit lonely, admiring how easy their belonging looked.

qa.q: What choice inside the story might have changed things for Naren?
qa.a: He could have joined the trekking club anyway and told his friends that making another friend did not mean leaving them.

qa.q: What was it like for Naren to be teased with "Leaving us?"
qa.a: He likely felt torn and pressured, wanting to try something new but afraid of seeming disloyal to the group.

grounding: An elder, Chetan, recalls watching a close hostel group from outside, noticing both its comfort and the unspoken pressure on members not to seek other friends.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
Shankar moved into the engineering hostel in October, two months late, because of a delay with his scholarship papers. By then the groups were already made.

He noticed Akash's group first: five of them, always at the corner table in the mess, always walking to class in a line, always in Akash's room at night with music playing.

Then the water supply failed for three days during midterms, and everyone had to queue at the one tap near the gate. Standing behind them, Shankar heard one of the five, Faizan, mention that he'd been invited to a study group with the second-years.

"You're going?" Akash asked lightly.

Faizan glanced at the others. "Nah. Just saying."

Shankar watched Faizan's face fall a little as he said it. Nobody had told him not to go. Nobody needed to.

qa.q: Why did Shankar move into the hostel two months late?
qa.a: Because of a delay with his scholarship papers.

qa.q: What does Shankar seem to feel watching the group from the tap queue?
qa.a: He seems curious and a bit lonely as the latecomer, and uneasy when he notices Faizan's face fall.

qa.q: How could Faizan's friends make room for him to try other groups?
qa.a: One of them could say, "Go, tell us how it is," so going to the study group would not feel like leaving them.

qa.q: What is it like for Faizan when Akash asks "You're going?" lightly?
qa.a: He feels a quiet pressure and disappointment, sensing that going would look disloyal even though no one forbade it.

grounding: Shankar, an outsider in a hostel, notices the comfort of Akash's tight group and the unspoken pressure that keeps Faizan from seeking other friends.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
Vikas had been Kamal's flatmate in Andheri for a month, and he still hadn't worked out how to join the others.

Kamal's college friends came over every Friday: the same four, the same order of seats on the sofa, the same takeaway biryani split five ways. They finished each other's stories. They had nicknames for everyone. Vikas liked watching them; it looked warm.

One Friday Kamal mentioned that a colleague had invited him to a pottery class on Saturdays.

"Pottery?" said one of them. "Since when are you an artist?"

"You'll miss our Saturday cricket," said another.

Kamal laughed it off. "I'm not going anyway."

But later, while clearing plates, Vikas saw Kamal look at the class brochure for a long moment before putting it in the drawer.

qa.q: What did Kamal's friends eat every Friday?
qa.a: Takeaway biryani split five ways.

qa.q: What does Kamal's long look at the brochure suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels disappointed and torn, wanting to try the pottery class but pressured by the group to stay.

qa.q: What small step could Kamal take?
qa.a: He could tell his friends that he'll try the pottery class for a few weeks and still join Saturday cricket when he can, so both are possible.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the group from outside?
qa.a: Vikas finds it warm and a little hard to enter, and notices the quiet pressure on Kamal that the group itself may not see.

grounding: Vikas, a new flatmate, observes the comfort of Kamal's college group and the unspoken pressure that makes Kamal put away a new interest.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
"Do they ever do anything alone?" Shreya asked, nodding at the table by the canteen window.

Nitin looked up from his samosa. "Who, my lot?"

"Your lot. Five of you. Breakfast together, library together, you all went to Rishikesh together. I transferred in August and I've never seen one of you without the other four."

Nitin laughed. "It's nice, na? You always have people."

"It looks nice. But when I asked Tanmay to join the photography club, he said, 'The group won't like it.' Like it's a rule."

Nitin paused, samosa halfway. "Nobody said that."

"Nobody has to say it."

He looked at the table, where the others were saving his chair. "Maybe. I did skip the theatre workshop because they'd all be at the movie."

Shreya shrugged. "Just saying. From outside, it's cosy. And a bit tight."

qa.q: When did Shreya transfer?
qa.a: Shreya transferred in August.

qa.q: What might Shreya be feeling as she watches the group?
qa.a: Shreya seems curious and a little wistful, admiring the closeness but uneasy about how tight it looks.

qa.q: What could Nitin try, based on this conversation?
qa.a: He could join the theatre workshop or another activity on his own, and say openly to the group that seeing other friends is okay.

qa.q: How does Nitin see his group at first, and what changes?
qa.a: At first he sees only the comfort of always having people; then he realises he has skipped things to stay with them.

grounding: An outsider notices a close college group doing everything together, comforting but carrying unspoken pressure not to seek other friends.
